Professional Game Engines (3D to 2D)
All have free versions with commercial options
Unity3D
Unreal Engine 5+
Godot
CryEngine
Lumberyard
Monogame
Marmalade

Unity3D
Flexible GameObject and Component Architecture on top of Monodevelop
Pros
C# or Visual Scripting
VR Friendly – engine of choice for many VR hardware manufacturers
Some automatic optimisationMultiple platform builds
Large Support Community and tutorials
Wide range of free and paid assets
Now has real time Global Illumination system
Very fast for prototyping
Cons
Not as powerful as UE6
WebGL code will be larger – there are options such as Needle Tools to build
Shader, Lighting systems lagging behind UE5
Has a more entry level feel – limited modelling and building

Unreal Engine 5+
C++ in Unreal’s Blueprint visual scripting system
Pros
Complete game development toolset
Professional engine choice
Powerful and expandable
C++ blueprint base
High end dynamic real time Lighting and Shading
High number of particles
Cons
Steeper Learning Curve than other engines
Slower to support VR
Heavier to run and not always ideal for mobile games

Overview
Unreal tended to be the market standard, but Unity has seemed to surpass it. It offers modular assets that cover any weak spots in the program, PhysX, a new GI PBR based system, and is the engine of choice for many new VR hardware manufacturers
https://unity3d.com/public-relations
Why?
Just good enough
Flexible marketplace additions – developer opportunity
Decreases code complexity (C#)
Large code library
Workflow is very streamlined - Iteration is fast
Multiple platforms
Solid and reliable – comfortable
Large support community
Overall strategy of inclusiveness
https://www.quora.com/Why-is-Unity-Game-Engine-so-successful

Unity3D Install 
Must have personal account – free for our purposes
Can have multiple versions installed – Via Unity Hub
Some Unity Hub Tutorials are in 2020.3f
Module Uses 6000.0.55f1 – it is the only version supported for the duration of the module in order to minimise issues
Projects must Use 6000.0.55f1 
Must open projects in correct versions

Can work online or offline – login helps consolidate projects and
Hub DesktopSettings between machines, especially if using Github Website

This week covers:

Basic Architecture

User Interface

Concepts

Next Week: Basic Scripting in C#

Basic Architecture

If familiar, please work on brainstorming on:

Basic Architecture (File in Top Menu)
Creating Project:

You are prompted to create  2D or 3D
	3D Contains 2D elements as well – images, textures, sprites

You can swap at any time

For 2.5D, select 3D and set camera and scene view to orthographic

There is Physics and Physics 2D settings you can adjust in edit/preferences

Basic Architecture (Project Window)
Projects – projects are hierarchal folders created by Unity that
Contain all the assets of a work

Assets may include Scripts, Data files, Animations, 3D Mesh Objects
Fonts, Plugins, Materials,  Textures, 

The Project File on Disk has Assets Folder, which displays all the 
items above, as well as other folders for Library items, Project Settings, Temp files, Builds, other data, and other operational items.

They may contain Visual Studio  or VSCode files if these are used as an IDE.

Basic Architecture (Project Window)
Project Window in Unity

You may move or organise your files or folders in any way you see fit in the 
Unity Project  Window within the Unity UI.

If you do it here, Unity keeps track of your files and will create all necessary 
linkages without any work on your part.

Do Not move files within the project in the windows interface, as this will 
Break the linkages above.

The Project Window may also contain shortcuts for certain files at the top

Basic Architecture (Scenes, Builds)
Scenes – these double up in Unity as Levels, and are sometimes
referred to as such. There is a SceneManager class you can use if desired.

Scenes are saved in the Assets Folder and appear in the project Window.

Builds – in build Settings you can select scenes (levels) to add to the export. 
It will play the first scene unless scripts otherwise specify. You may export to 
any Platform that is loaded. Install any platforms required at install stage or 
now, as these are all optional, apart from a PC build.

Build Platforms include: Webplayer (deprecated, now WebGL/GPU), Standalone (exe), Android, iOS, tvOS,  Tizen,  Xbox, PS, Windows Store, and Samsung TV

Basic Architecture (Top Menu)
Edit - These are a very basic set of functions and preferences

Preferences/External Tools:

IDE (Integrated Development Environment)- You can change IDE from Monodevelop to Visual Studio or VS Code in Preferences/External Tools. We will use Visual Studio.
Image Editing Program Options – Open by Individual File
Android SDK - Also has the android SDK link to set up if you have that installed.
Version Control:
	Visual Studio and Github Web – This is seamless and straightforward for linking with Unity. You will have to setup Github accounts, and it may be a good idea to have a Group github account that all have a password for. From anywhere you work you can pull down projects, work on them, and push changes back up to the account as separate commits.

Basic Architecture (Top Menu)
Edit: These are a very basic set of functions, build modules and preferences.

Assets: All standard Assets packages from the Unity library can be created here, or downloaded or custom packages installed.

GameObject (Empty Node) : This is the basic node used in Unity and is generic. From here you can create all library GameObjects from Unity 

Component (Script): This is a drop down menu of all Unity Components. This mirrors the Add Component button in the Inspector Window

Window: Typical windows besides the default to use are Game, Animator, 
and Lighting. The Window menu also provides access to the asset store. Typically you will purchase and load packages directly through this window into Unity

Basic Architecture (Hierarchy Window)

This is your working directory - List of Game Objects in Scene.

Drag items from Projects window into here or Scene View.

Re-Order by dragging up and down.

Can drag to other GameObjects to make child/parent.

Basic Architecture (GameObjects)

GameObjects are the fundamental objects in Unity that represent characters, props, and scenery.

They do not accomplish much in themselves, but they act as containers for Components(Scripts), which implement the real functionality.

Basic Architecture (GameObjects)

GameObjects and Components:
Base GameObject has name, tag, layer, and transform component
Scripts Are Components and define the empty GameObject
GameObjects and Components(Scripts) are Initialised and run when play is pressed 

Scripts must be attached to a GameObject in order for scripts to run (more later).
Scripts can be attached to an Empty gameObject.

All GameObjects Components and Scripts in scene(s) in build
Are available to run if accessed and visible. 

GameObjects will have variable and references that can be modified.
References can be to any Components, GameObjects, or Assets.

Could create all elements from empty GO
https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/class-GameObject.html

Unity is initialised and run from the Main Camera object.
This is the minimum requirement in order to build and run a scene/level.

Basic Architecture (Components)

Components are scripts, either pre-defined library or user defined

GameObjects will come with default Components(scripts) depending on 
Type, and these define the blank GameObject.

The Transform Component is the basic GameObject Component, 
Along with name, tag, and layer.

Basic Architecture (Inspector Window)

GameObjects, Scripts, and other assets are available for review and change in the Inspector Window. This exposes the individual components attached. You can add, remove, toggle active mode, or change and add/subtract parameters that are exposed. 

Public script variables declared are exposed here for value input or links to other game objects by drag and drop.

References to data files or other GameObjects may be exposed by the script and available here.

Components are added at the bottom.

Basic Architecture (Inspector Window)

Some default and possible library/added components include:
Name
Visibility – Turns object on and off. Simple.
Static – Game information Precomputed for non moving object
Tag – Allows naming for scripts to access (Collisions)
Layer – Cameras, Lights, can render certain layers, Raycasting can ignore
	(Camera Culling Mask, Raycast Layermask)
Transform – translation, rotation, scaling
Mesh – has rendering options, materials
Collider

Basic Architecture (Scripts, Classes)

Scripts and Classes

MonoBehaviour is the base class every script derives from.
Using Javascript every script automatically derives from MonoBehaviour. 
When using C# or Boo you have to explicitly derive from MonoBehaviour.

Classes – derived from monobehaviour, which unity is built on. MonoBehaviour is the base class every script derives from. Using Javascript every script automatically derives from MonoBehaviour.  When using C# or Boo you have to explicitly derive from MonoBehaviour.

Basic Architecture 
(Scripts, Classes, NameSpaces)


Namespaces
Libraries of Classes provided by Unity,  third parties, or yourself.

Typical:
using UnityEngine;
using System.Collections;

Basic Architecture (Default Scene Views)

Scene – basic working 3D/2D view

Game – View from Main Camera

Basic Architecture (Default Scene Views)

Main Camera – causes scene to run
Directional Light – required

Cannot have two main cameras in name

Later we can have a look at 3PC and FPC Cameras

Basic Architecture (Assets, Packages)

Three basic kinds:
	Unity Own
	User Created
	Third Party

Unity comes with free assets and offers a library or premium 
(not free) assets

Basic Architecture (Assets, Packages)

Assets:
Can be any individual file elements previously discussed.
Can be Created  via Assets/Create/
Can be imported via Assets/Import New Asset

Packages:
These are any combinations of assets and can include anything in the normal range of assets or custom assets in combination.
Unity provides a library of asset packages for various customised approaches 
(2D, Cameras, Characters, CrossPlatformInput, Effects, Environment, ParticleSystems, Prototyping, Utility, Vehicles)

Basic Architecture (PreFabs)

Good for enemies, multiple objects, scenery that is repeated,
Slightly modified, or procedurally animated or scripted.

GameObject Template to create Instances – one edit affects all

Note: Dragging Asset into Hierarcy or Scene/Game View will create
An Instance – changes to asset will change this instance. However,
It is not a prefab unless you define it as such. So, there can be two Levels of instancing for edits.

Basic Architecture (PreFabs)

You can drag the prefab in or spawn it in your scripts
(instantiating at runtime)

Note: You can instantiate a Prefab from one line of code, with complete 
functionality. Creating equivalent GameObjects from code takes an average of 
five lines of code, but likely more.You can set up, test, and modify the Prefab 
quickly and easily in the Scene and Inspector.You can change the Prefab being 
instanced without changing the code that instantiates it. A simple rocket might 
be altered into a super-charged rocket, and no code changes are required.

https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/InstantiatingPrefabs.html

Basic Architecture (PreFab Example)

A robot exploding to many pieces:
The complete, operational robot is destroyed and replaced with a wrecked robot Prefab. This Prefab would consist of the robot split into many parts, all set up with Rigidbodies and Particle Systems of their own. This technique allows you to blow up a robot into many pieces, with just one line of code, replacing one object with a Prefab.

Basic Architecture (Controllers - MVC)
These are Components or Packages provided by Unity libraries that can be added to a GameObject to give custom behaviour. These may be imported as packages, have own interface, or be added as a component.

Animator: New System for handling animation 
(Add as Component, has Window with Visual interface, Use Inspector on Animation to preview in first instance) 
Character: System for Navigation and player animation
(Import Character Package,  has Prefabs FPC and 3PC)
Scripts: Various scripts can also act as controllers
http://wiki.unity3d.com/index.php/Scripts/Controllers#Animation_Controllers

Basic Architecture (Scripts)
These are added as components and are available for access
By any GameObject or other Script if desired. Methods (Functions)  and variables can be accessed if desired.

It is not necessary to define the start script, as all scripts are called when built and run.

By default, the Awake, OnEnable and Update functions of different scripts are called in the order the scripts are loaded (which is arbitrary). However, it is possible to modify this order using the Script Execution Order settings (menu: Edit > Project Settings > Script Execution Order).

Mechanim

Also legacy Animation

Can co-exist as component controllers in different GameObjects in the scene.

PBR GI

Skybox
Click on the Assets folder in the project view
Using the top menu bar, select Assets/Create/Material. This will create a new material object in the assets folder
Rename the new material as Skybox
Select the Skybox Asset in the project view
In the inspector view, The Shader  option is defaulted to standard. Change that to Skybox/6 sided. This will create 6 textural slots for your new material.

Working in Unity

Create Login if needed, but can work offline
Download and Use Unity 6000.0.55f for duration of Module

Working in Unity (Toolbar)

Basic Controls
Scene Window:
	Toolbar top left has pan, translate, scale, box transform
	Transform Gizmos:
		Pivot or centre
		Local or Global 

Unity overlays a global coordinate system that may have a 
different location pivot to the objects own 
(we covered this last week with pivots)

Working in Unity (Play Mode)

Can be in Game Window or Full screen. View is from camera

When in Play mode, public variables and other exposed settings
May be adjusted for experimentation.

Please note: These changes are not saved, so if you want to 
Keep them, you must then adjust in the project after you exit
Play mode.

Console window shows Errors and script lines the occur on

Working in Unity ( IDEs)

Monodevelop IDE – Deprecated

Visual Studio IDE – Now preferred option, works well with Github Website

VS Code IDE also works, and is lighter, works well with Github Desktop, but takes further setup for full options.

Working in Unity (C# and OOP Concepts)
Classes, namespaces
Each script that you create will by default inherit from MonoBehaviour. Each script that you create will also have two functions defined by default: Start() and Update().
The Start() function will be run only once at the start of the program. So any logic and data initializations that you need or want to do can be placed in the Start() function.
The Update() function is where most of the magic happens. This is the function that gets called continuously throughout the life of your game or simulation. This is the function where you will update your game objects. In short it is the function which will be called each frame before rendering the scene.

Unity (C#)

Dependencies
	Using UnityEngine: lets MainCamera be initiated.
Namespaces
	MonoBehaviour is a class in Namespace UnityEngine. 	Others are not Class Definitions.
Start and Update Functions
	Void means it does not return a value. 
	Start initializes, Update refreshes.

Unity (C#) Vs. C#

Unity provides a framework so that you don't have to work out input handling, graphics instance setup, game loop, game object handling, physics, rendering, lighting etc yourself.

https://www.reddit.com/r/Unity3D/comments/32wps3/is_c_in_unity_different_to_general_c/

Unity (C#) Vs. C#

Constructors (the method that initializes a class' data). You almost never use constructors in Unity (in fact you can't for the most part), but you use them everywhere in normal development.

https://www.reddit.com/r/Unity3D/comments/32wps3/is_c_in_unity_different_to_general_c/
